t: Prenatal care: dating, screening, teratogens and vaccines
sub: Every prenatal decision is anchored to gestational age: date the pregnancy first, then time each screen, avoid the teratogens, and give the vaccines that protect mother and newborn.

pretest.q: Which ultrasound measurement gives the most accurate gestational age?
o: Crown-rump length in the first trimester
Femur length in the third trimester
Fundal height at the first visit
pretest.why: Embryos of the same age are almost the same size, so the crown-rump length predicts age within 5 to 7 days. Fetal size varies more with each week, so later measurements drift by weeks and never overrule an early scan.

w.Femur length in the third trimester: Growth differences between fetuses widen as pregnancy advances, so late femur measurements can be off by three weeks and are used to follow growth, not to set dates.
w.Biparietal diameter at 30 weeks: By 30 weeks head size reflects each fetus's genetic growth potential, so the biparietal diameter can be wrong by two to three weeks and tracks growth rather than age.
w.Fundal height at the first visit: Early in pregnancy the uterus is still inside the pelvis, so fundal height is not measured until 20 weeks, when it roughly equals the gestational age in centimeters.

pretest.q: Which maternal serum marker is raised when a fetus has an open neural tube defect?
pretest.why: Alpha-fetoprotein is made by the fetal liver and yolk sac, and an open neural tube defect lets it leak into amniotic fluid and then maternal blood. Inhibin A, estriol and PAPP-A track placental function and aneuploidy instead.

w.Inhibin A: Inhibin A is made by the placenta and rises with trisomy 21 on the quad screen, but it does not change when fetal neural tissue is exposed.
w.Unconjugated estriol: Estriol is built from fetal adrenal precursors and falls in trisomies 21 and 18, so it signals aneuploidy rather than a leaking neural tube defect.
w.PAPP-A: PAPP-A is a first-trimester placental protein that is low in trisomies, so it screens for aneuploidy and does not respond to open neural tube defects.

pretest.q: Which vaccine must be withheld until after delivery in a pregnant patient?
o: Tetanus, diphtheria and acellular pertussis vaccine
pretest.why: The measles, mumps and rubella vaccine contains live attenuated viruses that could infect the fetus, so it waits until after delivery. The toxoid, inactivated and protein vaccines hold no replicating organism and are recommended.

w.Tetanus, diphtheria and acellular pertus: Tdap is a toxoid and protein vaccine, and the maternal antibody it induces crosses the placenta to protect the newborn from pertussis, so it is given every pregnancy.
w.Inactivated influenza vaccine: Inactivated influenza vaccine is safe in any trimester and lowers the risk of severe maternal illness, preterm birth and infant infection during the season.
w.Respiratory syncytial virus vaccine: The prefusion RSV vaccine given at 32 to 36 weeks is a protein subunit product; it raises maternal antibody that transfers to the infant before the season.

body: How is a pregnancy dated and named?

Gestational age counts from the first day of the **last menstrual period** (LMP), so it runs about two weeks ahead of conception. {{rp30_naegele|Naegele's rule}} gives the due date by adding 7 days to the LMP and subtracting 3 months, which assumes a regular 28-day cycle with ovulation on day 14. Irregular cycles or a forgotten LMP break that assumption, so ultrasound sets the date. The **crown-rump length** in the first trimester is the most accurate method, within about 5 to 7 days, because embryos of the same age are almost the same size. The ultrasound date replaces the LMP date when they differ by more than 5 days before 9 weeks or more than 7 days from 9 to 14 weeks. Later, the biparietal diameter, abdominal circumference and femur length date less precisely because fetal growth varies, so an early date is not revised.

Stages are named by gestational age: **term** begins at 37 weeks, **preterm** is before 37 weeks, and **post-term** is 42 weeks or later. A loss before 20 weeks is an abortion, and a birth at 20 weeks or later counts toward parity. History is recorded as {{rp30_tpal|G P TPAL}}: gravidity (G) counts every pregnancy including the current one, parity (P) counts births from 20 weeks, and the four TPAL digits are term births, preterm births, abortions and living children. A patient now pregnant with one term birth, one set of twins born at 34 weeks and one miscarriage, with three living children, is G4 P1113, because twins count as one birth.
Date the pregnancy before reading any screen

Every prenatal test is interpreted against gestational age: AFP climbs each week, hCG falls after 10 weeks, and the quad screen window is 15 to 22 weeks. A wrong due date makes a normal result look abnormal, so the crown-rump length comes first.

The first visit at 6 to 10 weeks builds the risk profile. The **obstetric history** records preterm births, cesareans and stillbirths. Family history and ancestry guide carrier screening for cystic fibrosis, spinal muscular atrophy and hemoglobinopathies, and the clinician asks about medications and substance use. Risk factors include maternal age under 17 or over 35, smoking, chronic hypertension, pregestational diabetes and obesity. A urine culture finds **asymptomatic bacteriuria**: progesterone relaxes the ureters and the enlarging uterus compresses them, so untreated bacteriuria often becomes pyelonephritis and triggers preterm labor.
Blood type and antibody screen, CBC, HIV, **HBsAg**, syphilis, hepatitis C, chlamydia, gonorrhea, rubella and varicella IgG, urine culture
Cell-free DNA, first-trimester screen, chorionic villus sampling
Heart, spine, brain, kidneys, abdominal wall
Glucose challenge test, repeat CBC, anti-D at 28 weeks if Rh-negative
Tdap, influenza in season, RSV vaccine at 32 to 36 weeks

Every visit measures **blood pressure** and weight, listens to the fetal heart rate and asks about symptoms and fetal movement, first felt as quickening at 18 to 20 weeks. From 20 weeks the fundal height in centimeters matches the gestational age in weeks, within 2 cm, until about 36 weeks: the fundus reaches the pubic symphysis at 12 weeks and the umbilicus at 20 weeks. A uterus larger or smaller than expected calls for ultrasound. The anatomy scan screens for structural anomalies, and congenital heart defects, the most common, prompt fetal echocardiography.
How do screens find aneuploidy and neural tube defects?

Every patient is offered aneuploidy screening, whatever her age. {{rp30_cfdna|Cell-free DNA}} from 10 weeks measures placental DNA fragments in maternal blood and is the most sensitive screen for **trisomy 21**, but it remains a screen. The first-trimester screen at 10 to 13 weeks combines {{rp30_nt|nuchal translucency}}, PAPP-A and hCG. The **quad screen** at 15 to 22 weeks measures AFP, estriol, hCG and inhibin A. Trisomy 21 lowers AFP and estriol and raises hCG and inhibin A, trisomy 18 lowers all four, and either trisomy raises nuchal translucency and lowers PAPP-A. A positive screen is confirmed by chorionic villus sampling at 10 to 13 weeks, which takes placental tissue, or amniocentesis from 15 weeks, which takes fetal cells.

**Alpha-fetoprotein** (AFP) is made by the fetal liver and yolk sac and leaks into amniotic fluid and maternal blood. It rises with an open neural tube defect, such as anencephaly or open spina bifida, and with an abdominal wall defect, either gastroschisis, with no covering sac, or omphalocele, covered by a membrane and often linked to aneuploidy. It also rises with twins, fetal death and underestimated gestational age, because AFP climbs weekly, and it falls with the trisomies. Closed defects do not leak, so AFP may stay normal. Amniotic fluid {{rp30_ache|acetylcholinesterase}} confirms an open neural tube defect.
Working up a high maternal AFP
Underestimated dates are the commonest benign cause, so ultrasound comes first to confirm age and count the fetuses.
A detailed scan can show open spina bifida, an abdominal wall defect, twins or fetal death, each of which explains the AFP.
Test the fluid if still unexplained
Amniocentesis measures amniotic fluid AFP and acetylcholinesterase, both raised when an open defect leaks into the fluid.
A confirmed defect leads to delivery planning at a center with neonatal surgery; folic acid 4 mg is advised before any later pregnancy.
Villus sampling cannot find a neural tube defect

Chorionic villus sampling takes placental tissue, so it gives a karyotype but no amniotic fluid for AFP or acetylcholinesterase, and a normal result does not exclude a neural tube defect. A raised maternal AFP is followed by ultrasound and, if needed, amniocentesis.

Folic acid supports DNA synthesis during rapid closure of the neural tube, which finishes about 28 days after conception, before many patients know they are pregnant. Every patient who could become pregnant therefore takes **0.4 mg** of folic acid daily, starting at least a month before conception and continuing through the first trimester, which cuts neural tube defects by roughly 70 percent. A preconception dose of **4 mg** daily is used after a pregnancy with a neural tube defect, and is often used with folate antagonists such as trimethoprim or carbamazepine.
Which exposures injure the embryo, and when?

Timing decides the injury. In the first 2 weeks after fertilization damage is all or none: the embryo either dies or recovers. During weeks 3 to 8, {{rp30_organogenesis|organogenesis}}, a teratogen causes major structural malformations, and each organ has its own window. After week 9 the fetal period brings growth restriction and functional injury, and the brain stays vulnerable throughout. A drug reaches the fetus when it is small, lipid soluble and un-ionized, which is why heparin and insulin, large and charged, stay in the mother.
Block angiotensin II, so fetal filtration fails: renal failure, **oligohydramnios**, pulmonary hypoplasia
Block prostaglandins that hold the ductus arteriosus open: premature closure
Blocks vitamin K carboxylation in bone: nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses
Interfere with folate use: neural tube defects
Folate antagonist: limb and craniofacial defects, fetal loss
Retinoic acid disrupts neural crest cells: craniofacial, cardiac and CNS defects
Bind calcium in forming teeth: yellow-brown discoloration
Damage inner-ear hair cells: eighth-nerve deafness
Disrupts neuronal migration and midface growth: smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, microcephaly

Lithium causes Ebstein anomaly and phenytoin causes hypoplastic nails and distal phalanges. **Methimazole** causes aplasia cutis and choanal atresia, so propylthiouracil is used in the first trimester. Misoprostol causes the Mobius sequence, mycophenolate causes microtia and clefts, and topiramate causes cleft lip. Diethylstilbestrol in utero causes vaginal clear cell adenocarcinoma. Alcohol causes {{rp30_fas|fetal alcohol syndrome}}; cocaine constricts placental vessels, causing abruption, preterm birth and low birth weight; and opioid use causes neonatal withdrawal, while maternal opioid use disorder is treated with methadone or buprenorphine. Radiation above 50 mGy and pregestational diabetes (caudal regression) are also teratogenic.
Why can heparin treat a pregnant patient when warfarin cannot?

Warfarin is a small, lipid-soluble molecule that crosses the placenta. There it blocks vitamin K-dependent carboxylation of clotting factors and bone proteins, so exposure at 6 to 12 weeks causes **nasal hypoplasia** and stippled epiphyses, and later exposure causes fetal bleeding and brain injury. Heparin is a large, strongly negatively charged polysaccharide, so it cannot cross the placenta and anticoagulates only the mother. A pregnant patient with venous thromboembolism therefore receives heparin.
Which vaccines are safe in pregnancy, and which are not?

Inactivated and toxoid vaccines are safe in any trimester, and three are routine. **Tdap** is given in every pregnancy at 27 to 36 weeks, because maternal IgG crosses the placenta and protects the newborn from pertussis until its own vaccines begin at 2 months; antibody fades, so the dose is repeated each time. Inactivated influenza vaccine is given in any trimester during the season, since influenza raises the risk of severe maternal illness and preterm birth. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccine is given at 32 to 36 weeks from September through January, or the infant receives an RSV antibody instead. **Live vaccines**, MMR, varicella and intranasal influenza, are contraindicated in pregnancy. Nonimmune patients are vaccinated after delivery, even when breastfeeding, and avoid conception for a month.

body.q: A newborn cannot receive pertussis vaccine until 2 months of age. Which reasoning best explains why Tdap is given at 27 to 36 weeks of every pregnancy?
o: Maternal IgG made after vaccination crosses the placenta late in pregnancy and protects the newborn until its own vaccines begin
The vaccine's live organisms replicate in the mother and prime fetal T cells to respond to pertussis after birth
Maternal IgM made after vaccination crosses the placenta in the third trimester and gives lasting immunity
Early vaccination lets the fetus make memory B cells before organogenesis ends, so timing matters little
body.why: Pertussis is most dangerous before the infant's own vaccines work. Tdap is an inactivated toxoid vaccine, so it is safe, and the maternal IgG it induces crosses the placenta through the neonatal Fc receptor, with transfer rising in the third trimester. Giving it at 27 to 36 weeks maximizes antibody at birth. IgM is too large to cross, and antibody wanes within a year, so the dose is repeated in every pregnancy.

grid.q: Which statements about prenatal care are correct?
items: Crown-rump length is the most accurate dating tool in the first trimester
Trisomy 21 gives low AFP, low estriol, high hCG and high inhibin A
Chorionic villus sampling cannot detect neural tube defects
Folic acid 4 mg is used after a prior neural tube defect
Tdap is given in every pregnancy at 27 to 36 weeks
ACE inhibitors cause fetal renal failure and oligohydramnios
Warfarin causes nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses
Heparin does not cross the placenta
MMR vaccine is given at 28 weeks
Open neural tube defects lower maternal serum AFP
Cell-free DNA is a diagnostic test
